what_happened.line: The Finance Committee agreed in principle to a monthly 'tri-board' process with the Select Board and School Committee to build the FY27 budget, starting in July.
Members reviewed ten years of district staffing data showing enrollment declined while total school staffing kept rising, including growth in paraprofessional and clerical positions.
A member said the district changed its accounting practice for out-of-district placement costs, which affected how that budget line appears to have grown between FY24 and now.
A resident spoke against the tri-board process, arguing a large joint meeting would accomplish little and citing difficulty getting financial information from the school department.
The committee set its next meeting for July 10, with none scheduled for June 26.

why_it_matters: A joint tri-board process would change how the FY27 school and town budgets are shaped before residents see a warrant article, potentially surfacing overrides or consolidations earlier than in past years.
The staffing-versus-enrollment questions raised touch the school budget's biggest cost driver and will likely resurface as documentation requests in the tri-board sessions.
A change in how out-of-district placement costs are accounted for affects how budget-to-budget comparisons on that line should be read, not necessarily how much is actually being spent.

meetings.headline: FinCom pressed the school committee on budget transparency and flagged growing revolving-fund deficits ahead of Town Meeting
meetings.summary: In its last meeting before Annual Town Meeting, the Finance Committee approved the consent calendar for town meeting, reviewed excluded-debt scenarios for the Marshall Park and municipal building projects, and heard extended public comment on free cash use, the school budget, and cemetery finances. Members spent much of the meeting criticizing the school department's budget transparency, citing unexplained line-item transfers and a growing athletic revolving-account deficit, and agreed to pursue records requests and a redesigned, earlier budget development timeline for next year.

The chair clarified, after initially misspeaking about Chapter 70, that Chapter 90 holds a balance over $2 million.
The chair said Chapter 70 aid has grown about 1.3% per year for the last four years, which everyone agrees needs addressing at the state level.
The chair said the town did not put money into stabilization this year and is effectively drawing down reserves for this one year, which is not best fiscal policy.
A member said last year's roughly one-million-dollar override went entirely to the school budget and remains there, compounding with the annual increase.
A member said that of 351 Massachusetts cities and towns, 16, including Lunenburg, passed an override designated for schools last year.

budget_items.topic: Town budget and tax rate sustainability
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident argued that a 2.5% annual increase and the current tax rate are unsustainable against a roughly $49 million town budget.
A resident explained cemetery fee mechanics, saying a cremation brings in a fee with nothing to perpetual care while a full burial is split between the burial-rights fund and perpetual care.
The same resident said the cemetery sale-of-lots account holds about $96,000 that is not visibly being used to improve the cemeteries.
The resident estimated roughly $6 per grave (or $4 a lot) to maintain about 6,000 graves, arguing current fees do not cover it.
The chair modeled scenarios showing excluded debt could reach about 12% against an 11% policy target if both the Marshall Park and municipal building debt exclusions pass.
The chair said the town was around 11% excluded debt in 2020 and was in excess of roughly 14% when the high school/middle school was built.
The chair modeled a hypothetical $110 million new Turkey Hill school with 50% MSBA reimbursement, netting about $55 million to the town, citing a $700 million Boston vocational school as context.
The chair said that over a 10-year period, excluding the override year, the town's tax levy actually grew about 4.2% per year on average, not just 2.5%.
The chair said the debt model assumed about 10% of the Marshall Park cost could be covered by grants.
A member said the reduced-scope Marshall Park proposal is priced at about $30 million and suggested asking the parks commission why that is the chosen scope.

budget_items.topic: School budget share of town budget
budget_items.what_was_said: A member said the school department is roughly 56% of the town's budget, making its lack of transparency a significant problem.
A member described watching a school committee meeting where a line-item transfer of roughly $16,000-$19,000 for copies was questioned but the underlying numbers were not spoken aloud.
A member reported the school athletic revolving account ran deficits of about $115,000 in 2024, $169,000 in 2023, and $120,000 this year, with the town covering the shortfall.
The same member said the athletic revolving account has run about $178,000 in the red cumulatively since 2020.
A member said the extended-day program does not fully cover its costs, with about $50,000 typically pulled from the school budget to cover it.
The chair said the town received about $880,000 last year, $690,000 the year before, and about $550,000 this year to cover school lunches, and funding would need to be found if that support ended.
A member said at least $120,000 of the roughly $948,000 override passed for the schools will go toward covering the FY25 athletic revolving account deficit.

budget_items.topic: School staffing cuts vs. budget increase
budget_items.what_was_said: A member described the confusing appearance of the school budget needing a 12% year-over-year increase while also cutting about 9% of staff and services.
A remote commenter called the town's $60,000 annual audit a poor use of money since it failed to catch known problems such as the parks revolving account.

budget_items.topic: Fire dept vehicle maintenance reserve fund transfer
budget_items.what_was_said: The fire chief requested a reserve fund transfer to cover an ambulance diesel particulate filter/exhaust repair after vehicle maintenance funds ran low. He noted the line typically covers fuel and one significant repair a year.

budget_items.topic: Article 2 - borrowing in anticipation of revenue
budget_items.what_was_said: A new fail-safe article to allow the town to borrow if there is a cash-flow shortfall from revenues not coming in as expected; select board recommended it at 50.
A variety of capital projects were bundled into one article, including a disputed $50,000 cemetery road item that a resident wanted redirected to electrical infrastructure instead.

budget_items.topic: Special projects funding / grant writing pilot (Article 9)
budget_items.what_was_said: Following prior discussion, crack-seal/cemetery road repairs were swapped out for a grant writing services pilot proposal in this article.
The town manager presented the omnibus budget total, unchanged from the prior presentation; the committee noted ongoing conversations with departments before town meeting.
A citizen's petition sought a Proposition 2½ override; select board voted not to recommend it and not to place it on the ballot, though it may still appear via the citizens' petition process.

budget_items.topic: $500,000 free cash transfer to schools, conditioned on override failing (Article 12)
budget_items.what_was_said: This transfer would only occur if the override fails; the committee deferred its recommendation pending a school presentation on how the money would be spent.

budget_items.topic: SAP grade adjustments - DPW director and communications/IT manager (Article 13)
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager said upgrading the DPW director's grade and expanding a part-time communications/IT position to full-time would each cost roughly $10,000, funded from the salary reserve line.

budget_items.topic: Insurance cost for new full-time position
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident noted that historically a $10,000 salary increase for a new full-time hire could carry roughly a $35,000 total budget impact once family health insurance is included.
The town manager's proposed non-union pay plan increase moved from 2.5% to 3%, an estimated $43,000 total impact, while the clerical union received a larger negotiated increase.
Paying call firefighters time-and-a-half for holiday shifts was estimated at up to $6,000 based on holidays falling on Sundays.
These free-cash-to-stabilization transfers are the ones being effectively redirected to fund the $500,000 school transfer; the committee recommended no action, following the select board.
A free cash transfer to the town's other-post-employment-benefits trust fund, which is only about 2.69% funded, was recommended as this should not be skipped.
A new reserve fund to cover unbudgeted accrued vacation/sick time payouts when employees separate, funded with $10,000 from free cash.
A bundle of sewer-enterprise transfers covering OPEB liability, the FY26 sewer operating budget, inflow/infiltration stabilization, and reserve capacity stabilization.
Pay-as-you-throw bag revenues fund the trash portion of the solid waste program; a bag price increase was flagged as a likely future discussion.
A transfer from water enterprise revenues to operate the water enterprise fund for FY26.
The public access program is drawing down its reserves this year by roughly $30,000 and is expected to need closer attention as cable-based revenue continues to decline.

A debt exclusion requiring both town meeting and ballot approval; estimated tax rate impact ranged by amortization term, with the chair's own debt-capacity analysis showing the town stays within its 11% excludable debt policy in most years.

budget_items.topic: Municipal building / Ritter Memorial renovation debt exclusion (Article 34)
budget_items.what_was_said: A debt exclusion to renovate town hall into a meeting house and expand Ritter building for municipal and school offices; residents raised concerns about unknown future operating costs and contingency adequacy.

budget_items.topic: Tax rate impact of the school override (annual report)

meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Finance Committee received an update from the superintendent on changes to the school department's FY26 budget since a March 6th presentation, covering transportation, staffing restructurings, health insurance, and a new bus fee. Much of the meeting was consumed by a contentious debate over the athletic department's proposal to run fee-based summer camps, which one member strongly opposed as redundant with the town's Recreation Department; no vote was taken on the camps issue. what_happened.line: The Finance Committee voted by roll call to recommend a reserve fund transfer to the school department for unbudgeted enhanced 911 cabling.
The town manager did not present a preliminary budget, citing errors in the revenue estimates, and hopes to present the full budget on Feb 27.
The town manager said the 2.5 percent increase was not applied to the levy including the override, which leaves more revenue than first thought.
The IT department presented its FY26 budget items, including a rising MUNIS contract as the system moves to the cloud.
Departments were asked to supply full budgets with prior-year actuals in a standardized Excel format.

why_it_matters: The reserve fund was set at Town Meeting for the committee to release, so each transfer, including this one, leaves less in it for the rest of the year.
The FY26 revenue estimate has changed since it was first built, and the preliminary budget that residents and Town Meeting will vote on comes later than first expected.

The January 23 meeting will be held only if something pressing comes up; otherwise the next meeting is February 13.

why_it_matters: The dates set here decide when the school and town budgets get a hearing and when a resident can speak before the committee votes and Town Meeting.
Health insurance is a cost the town does not yet have a figure for, so the FY26 budget could change once rates arrive.
A resident said he will propose a warrant article on cemetery commission spending, which would be a vote residents may be asked to take at Town Meeting.
